replace_covers.math.addition-subtraction.meaning.L2: Addition and subtraction undo each other: fact families (7 + 5 = 12, 12 − 5 = 7); subtraction as finding the difference as well as taking away; missing-number problems to 20 and with tens to 100.
replace_covers.math.addition-subtraction.mental-strateg: Adding and subtracting 2-digit numbers in the head: splitting into tens and ones, jumping along an empty number line, adding 9 by adding 10 and taking 1 back.

Compensating (398 + 247 as 400 + 247 − 2), partitioning and using known facts with 3- and 4-digit numbers; adding and subtracting multiples of 10, 100 and 1000; explaining which way is quicker and why.

Mental methods with large numbers and with decimals (tenths and hundredths, as in money); choosing between rounding and adjusting, splitting, and counting up; estimating first and checking the answer against the estimate.
Multi-step problems from real life (bills, journeys, populations) that mix all four operations and decimals; deciding what is asked, what is needed and what is extra; writing the steps as one number sentence with brackets.
replace_covers.math.addition-subtraction.written-method: Adding and subtracting numbers in lakhs and crores (travel distances, populations) and decimals in columns, lining up the decimal point; estimating first; checking with the inverse.
replace_covers.math.data.bar-charts.L5: Choosing how to show data and choosing the scale; double bar charts that compare two groups; bar charts of experiment results; saying what the chart shows and what it cannot show.
replace_covers.math.data.line-graphs.L5: Drawing line graphs with chosen scales on both axes; reading values between the plotted points; steep and gentle slopes as fast and slow change; spotting a trend and making a careful prediction from it.
replace_covers.math.data.pictographs.L5: Data Through Pictures: pictographs with a key and part-pictures (half a picture for 5 when one stands for 10); turning a table into a pictograph and into a bar chart and judging which shows the data better.
replace_covers.math.data.reading-data.L4: What does the data tell us? Comparing two groups from tables and charts; the most, the least and the difference; telling what the data shows from what we only guess.
replace_covers.math.data.reading-data.L5: The same data told two ways; using averages (mean, median, mode) and range to compare two sets; how a graph can mislead (a cut-off scale, pictures drawn too big, a chosen stretch of time, a hidden total); redrawing a misleading graph honestly; asking who collected the data and why.
Tenths as decimals: 0.1 is one of ten equal parts; tenths on a ruler and a number line; rupees and paise and metres and centimetres written with a decimal point; comparing decimals with one place.

Tenths, hundredths and thousandths as places to the right of the ones; comparing and ordering decimals; rounding to the nearest whole number and tenth; fractions, decimals and percentages (out of 100) as three ways to write one number; simple ratio (for every).
replace_covers.math.fractions.fractions-of-a-whole.L4: Sharing and measuring with fractions; equivalent fractions with strips (1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8); comparing fractions with the same top or the same bottom number; adding and subtracting fractions with the same denominator.
replace_covers.math.fractions.fractions-of-a-whole.L5: Comparing and ordering fractions by making the denominators the same; simplest form; improper fractions and mixed numbers; adding and subtracting fractions whose denominators are the same or multiples of each other; a fraction of a quantity (3/4 of 60).
replace_covers.math.fractions.halves-and-quarters.L2: Halves and quarters of shapes and sets; two quarters make a half; the parts must be equal in size but need not look the same.
replace_covers.math.fractions.ratio-and-proportion.L4: For every 2 cups of rice, 1 cup of dal: recipes and mixing paint; ratio compares by 'for every', not by 'how many more'; tables of equal ratios; keeping the taste or shade the same when making more.
replace_covers.math.fractions.ratio-and-proportion.L5: Ratio written a:b and simplified; sharing an amount in a given ratio; direct proportion and the unitary method (find the value of one first); scaling recipes up and down; maps and models to scale.
replace_covers.math.logic.counting-ways.L5: Arrangements where order matters (4 children in a line: 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 ways) and choices where it does not (pairs chosen from 5 children); why the two counts differ; the multiplication rule; discrete maths, the maths of countable things. Networks and the bridges of Königsberg now have their own units.
replace_covers.math.logic.if-then.L5: Chains of if-then steps (if A then B, if B then C, so if A then C); why 'if it rains the road is wet' does not mean 'if the road is wet it rained'; one counter-example is enough to show a rule is false.
replace_covers.math.logic.puzzles.L5: Logic grid puzzles solved by ruling out; working backwards from the end; puzzles from Indian mathematics (Bhaskara's Lilavati); writing your own puzzle with exactly one answer.
replace_covers.math.logic.sets-and-venn.L4: Venn diagrams with two and three circles and Carroll diagrams (yes/no tables); placing numbers by two properties (even, multiple of 3); what the overlap and the outside mean.
replace_covers.math.maths-and-world.maths-and-art.L5: The golden ratio found from the Fibonacci numbers (divide each by the one before); where it truly appears and where the claim is a myth; perspective drawing with a vanishing point; drawing with coordinates. Rhythm and notes now have their own units.
replace_covers.math.maths-and-world.maths-and-science.L: Rates and compound measures used in science: speed = distance ÷ time, density, and ratio in recipes and mixtures; scale models; writing a relationship as a formula and testing it against measurements.
replace_covers.math.maths-and-world.what-is-maths.L5: Is maths discovered or invented? What a proof is and why it matters: mathematicians do not accept 'it worked every time I tried'; the starting rules are chosen by people, and what follows from them is not.
replace_covers.math.measurement-basics.scale-models.L4: Scale drawings: 1 cm stands for 1 m; drawing a room to scale on squared paper and finding real lengths from the drawing.
replace_covers.math.money.money-in-life.L4: Making a budget for a week or a trip; comparing prices; bills with several items, using decimals; rounding to estimate a total before paying.
replace_covers.math.number-sense.history-of-numbers.L5: How the place-value system with zero travelled from India through the Arab world to Europe, and why it replaced Roman numerals; numbers in other bases; what the usual story leaves out.
replace_covers.math.number-sense.infinity.L3: Numbers never end: whatever number you name, adding 1 makes a bigger one, so there is no biggest number; counting down below zero never ends either; patterns that go on for ever.
replace_covers.math.number-sense.infinity.L5: Infinity is an idea, not a number you can reach; endless halving (1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... gets as close to 1 as you like and never passes it); endlessly many fractions between any two numbers; endless patterns; the surprise, found by Georg Cantor, that some infinities are bigger than others.
replace_covers.math.number-sense.negative-numbers.L5: Ordering negative numbers; temperature differences across zero; adding and subtracting with negative numbers as moves along the number line; fortunes and debts, the way Brahmagupta wrote the rules.
replace_covers.math.number-sense.powers-and-roots.L4: Square numbers as squares of dots and cube numbers as cubes of blocks; doubling again and again (powers of 2) and how fast it grows; writing 2 × 2 × 2 as 2³.
replace_covers.math.number-sense.powers-and-roots.L5: Powers of ten and other powers written with an index; square roots as 'which number times itself?', and placing roots that are not whole numbers between two whole numbers (the root of 20 lies between 4 and 5); cube roots of small cubes; the chessboard and rice story.
replace_covers.math.number-sense.zero.L3: Zero as a placeholder in 3-digit numbers (305 is not 35); India's gift of zero as a number; adding and subtracting zero; multiplying by zero gives zero, and why.
replace_covers.math.patterns.number-patterns.L4: Pattern Around Us: growing patterns; rules for patterns said in words (start at 3, add 4 each time); finding the 10th term without writing them all.
replace_covers.math.patterns.number-patterns.L5: Sequences and their rules: the rule from one term to the next and the rule from the position (the nth term is 3 × n + 1); square and triangle numbers, and why two neighbouring triangle numbers make a square.
replace_covers.math.patterns.shape-patterns.L4: Pattern Around Us: patterns in shapes: growing shape patterns (matchstick squares) counted in a table; tile patterns made by turning and flipping.
replace_covers.math.patterns.shape-patterns.L5: Shapes and Patterns; spirals, fractals and the Fibonacci numbers in nature; a shape pattern turned into a number rule, with the rule explained from the picture.
replace_covers.math.position.coordinates.L5: Coordinates on a grid in all four quadrants, using negative numbers; plotting points; drawing pictures with coordinates; finding the missing corner of a rectangle; distances between points on the same grid line.
replace_covers.math.probability.likely-and-unlikely.L2: Certain, maybe, impossible: sorting everyday events into three groups and giving a reason.
replace_covers.math.probability.likely-and-unlikely.L4: Likely, unlikely, even chance; the language of chance placed on a line from impossible (0) to certain (1) with a half in the middle; comparing two chances and explaining why.
replace_covers.math.probability.experiments.L5: Predicting from experiments: the fraction of times something happened as an estimate of its chance (probability as a fraction); things with no neat answer in advance (a dropped spoon, a bottle cap); comparing the experiment with the counted chance in Ludo and snakes and ladders.
replace_covers.math.shapes-2d.polygons-and-properties.L: Shapes and Patterns: triangles sorted by sides and by angles; the family of quadrilaterals (parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle, square, trapezium, kite) and how one is a special case of another; diagonals; circles: centre, radius, diameter.
replace_covers.math.shapes-3d.nets.L4: Unfolding a box; nets of a cube: finding the 11 different nets by trying; which arrangements of 6 squares do not fold into a cube, and why.
replace_covers.math.algebra.balance-and-missing-numbers: Number sentences with a box for the unknown in any position (□ + 8 = 15, 20 − □ = 6, 3 × □ = 12); true and false number sentences; the equals sign as 'is the same as'.

Simple equations as balance puzzles with letters for unknown numbers; two-step equations (2x + 3 = 11) solved by doing the same to both sides; the unknown on both sides (3x + 2 = x + 10); checking by putting the answer back.
replace_covers.math.algebra.input-output.L3: Number machines: what's the rule? Finding it from pairs of inputs and outputs (add, subtract or multiply); making a machine for a partner to crack.
replace_covers.math.algebra.input-output.L5: Rules with two steps written with a letter (n → 2 × n + 1); finding the input from the output; two different-looking machines that always give the same output, and why.
replace_covers.math.division.division-facts.L4: Dividing 2-digit numbers by a 1-digit number; remainders; checking with multiplication (quotient × divisor + remainder).
replace_covers.math.division.division-facts.L5: Dividing by 1- and 2-digit numbers (long division); Coconut Farm; what to do with a remainder depends on the story: round up, round down, or share it out as a fraction.
replace_covers.math.lines-angles.angles.L4: Right angles as quarter turns, tested with a folded paper corner; angles smaller and bigger than a right angle (acute and obtuse); half a right angle; angles made by clock hands.
replace_covers.math.lines-angles.angles.L5: Angles as Turns: right, acute, obtuse and straight angles; comparing angles by laying one on another (the length of the arms does not matter); degrees in simple words: a full turn is 360, a right angle 90.
Measuring a tree's height with its shadow and a stick (similar triangles: the same shape, with sides in the same ratio); measuring a height by sighting along a folded paper triangle; how surveyors measured Everest; the idea behind trigonometry.
replace_covers.math.symmetry.rotational-symmetry.L5: Order of rotational symmetry; designs that turn; shapes with turning symmetry but no mirror line.
replace_covers.math.symmetry.transformations.L5: Tessellations: which shapes cover a floor with no gaps, and why (the angles round a point must add up to 360 degrees); the only three regular tilings; making your own tile by cutting and sliding; transformations in art and tiles.
replace_covers.math.area-perimeter.area.L4: Area by counting squares, including half squares; square centimetres; shapes that look different and have the same area.
replace_covers.math.area-perimeter.area.L5: Area of rectangles as length × breadth, and of L-shapes and other composite shapes by splitting into rectangles; square centimetres and square metres; same perimeter, different area, and same area, different perimeter (Grandmother's Quilt).
replace_covers.math.area-perimeter.volume.L5: Volume by counting cubes, then length × breadth × height for a box; cubic centimetres; capacity and volume: 1 litre fills a 10 cm cube; the volume of a stone from the water it pushes up.
replace_covers.math.big-ideas.change-and-motion.L4: How fast is it going right now? Average speed over a trip against speed at one moment; a steeper distance-time graph means faster; shrinking the time gap to get closer to 'right now'.
replace_covers.math.big-ideas.change-and-motion.L5: Adding up thin slices to find an area with a curved edge, and why thinner slices give a better answer; change and continuity; rate of change as the steepness of a graph; how equations describe changing things (rockets, populations); the idea behind calculus, from the endless sums of Madhava's Kerala school to Newton and Leibniz.
replace_covers.math.factors-multiples.factors-and-multi: Multiples on a number line; animal jumps; common multiples; factors as the numbers that divide exactly; all the factor pairs of numbers to 50, found with arrays.
Factors and multiples; primes and composites; tests of divisibility; finding every factor of a number to 100 in order and knowing when to stop; perfect numbers (6 and 28).

add.subject: math
add.name: Zero holds the place
add.covers: Zero as the keeper of an empty place: 10, 20 and 100 built with bundles and an empty ones box; why 1, 10 and 100 are different numbers; zero as the starting point of the number line and of a ruler. The child can say what each zero in a number is doing.

add.subject: math
add.name: Zero's long journey
add.covers: How zero became a number: empty-place marks in older systems, then Brahmagupta's written rules for working with zero (628 CE), then its travel through the Arab world to Europe, where many people resisted it. Why dividing by zero gives no answer (no number times 0 makes 5), shown by trying. The child can explain why zero is both a digit and a number, and why we cannot divide by it.

add.subject: math
add.name: The hotel with endless rooms
add.covers: Hilbert's hotel: a full hotel with endlessly many rooms can still take one more guest, and even endlessly many more, by moving everyone along. Pairing as the way to compare endless collections: the even numbers can be paired one-to-one with all the counting numbers, so there are 'as many' of each. The child can show a pairing and say why the usual rule 'a part is smaller than the whole' fails for endless sets.
verify: Hilbert's hotel is usually dated to a 1924 lecture by David Hilbert; check the date before printing it in the unit.

add.subject: math
add.name: Other ways to write numbers
add.covers: Number systems side by side: Roman numerals to 1000 and why sums are hard without place value; the Babylonian system built on 60, still alive in our minutes and seconds; the Maya system built on 20, with its own zero. Writing the same number in each. The child can read and write Roman numerals and explain what a base is.

add.subject: math
add.name: Counting in twos and fives: number bases
add.covers: Place value works in any base: grouping in fives (hands) and in twos (binary); place values 1, 2, 4, 8, 16; changing numbers to 31 and beyond between base ten and base two; adding in binary; why computers use binary (on and off). The child can convert both ways and explain that base ten is a choice people made, not a law.

add.subject: math
add.name: Square numbers
add.covers: Square numbers made as squares of dots and tiles up to 10 × 10; a number times itself; adding the odd numbers in order (1, 1 + 3, 1 + 3 + 5) always gives a square, seen by adding an L-shaped border. The child can list the squares to 100 and show with dots why the odd numbers build them.

add.subject: math
add.name: How big is a thousand?
add.covers: Getting a feel for 1000: a thousand steps, seconds, grains and rupees; building 1000 from ten hundreds; estimating which things come in hundreds and which in thousands. The child can say how long, how heavy or how far a thousand of something is.

add.subject: math
add.name: Very small numbers
add.covers: Going down in tens: tenths, hundredths, thousandths and millionths; millimetres and micrometres; the sizes of a hair, a cell and a virus compared; each step ten times smaller, the mirror image of the big-number ladder. The child can order very small lengths and say how many times smaller one is than another.

add.subject: math
add.name: Good guesses: rounding to the nearest ten
add.covers: Rounding 2- and 3-digit numbers to the nearest 10 and 100 on a number line; estimating a sum or difference before working it out; estimating a jarful by counting one handful. The child can give a sensible estimate and say whether an exact answer is reasonable.

add.subject: math
add.name: Families of numbers
add.covers: How the number family grew each time a sum had no answer: counting numbers, zero, negative numbers, fractions. Between any two fractions there is always another. Then numbers that are not fractions at all: the diagonal of a 1 by 1 square (the square root of 2) and pi, whose decimals never end and never settle into a repeat. Stated as found, with the proof left for later years. The child can place each kind on the number line and say which sum forced it into being.

add.subject: math
add.name: Story sums with bigger numbers
add.covers: One-step stories with numbers to 100: adding to, taking from, putting together and comparing (how many more?); drawing a bar picture of the story before choosing to add or subtract. The child can draw the story and write its number sentence.

add.subject: math
add.name: Bar models for harder stories
add.covers: Two- and three-step problems with 4-digit numbers, solved with bar models: comparison (A has 250 more than B, together they have 1750), before-and-after, and part-whole with a missing part. The child can solve a problem where the first answer is only a step to the second, and check that the result fits the story.

add.subject: math
add.name: Splitting and regrouping to multiply
add.covers: The distributive law seen in arrays: 7 × 12 is 7 × 10 and 7 × 2; grouping three numbers in any order (2 × 7 × 5 done as 7 × 10); multiplying by 0 and by 1. The child can break a hard product into easy ones and show with an array why it works.

add.subject: math
add.name: Times as many: multiplying as scaling
add.covers: Multiplication as stretching, not only as groups: 3 times as long, 5 times as heavy; comparison problems (Ravi has 4 times as many as Mala; how many more?); halving and doubling a recipe. The child can tell 'times as many' from 'more than' and solve comparison problems with a bar model.

add.subject: math
add.name: Many ways to multiply
add.covers: The same product worked four ways: the grid, the standard method, the lattice (boxes with diagonals) and the doubling-and-halving method used in ancient Egypt. Each one is the distributive law written differently; the child finds where each partial product hides. The child can use two methods, explain why both give the same answer, and say that the 'standard' method is a choice.

add.subject: math
add.name: Remainders that go round
add.covers: Remainders repeat in a cycle: dividing 1, 2, 3 ... by 4 gives remainders 1, 2, 3, 0 again and again; odd and even as remainder 1 or 0 on dividing by 2; using remainders to find the day of the week 30 days from now or the colour of the 50th bead. The child can use a remainder to predict far along a repeating cycle.

add.subject: math
add.name: Clock arithmetic
add.covers: Arithmetic on a circle: on a 12-hour clock 9 + 5 = 2; adding and multiplying using only remainders; why the remainder of a sum can be found from the remainders of its parts; uses in calendars (the weekday of a date) and in the check digit on a book's barcode. The child can add and multiply on a clock of any size and explain that 'the same' here means 'leaves the same remainder'.

add.subject: math
add.name: Dividing on: answers with fractions and decimals
add.covers: When the remainder is shared too: 7 ÷ 2 as 3 remainder 1, as 3 1/2 and as 3.5; a fraction is a division (3/4 is 3 ÷ 4); dividing on into tenths and hundredths; 1 ÷ 3 gives 0.333... which never ends. The child can give a division answer in the form the story needs and turn simple fractions into decimals.

add.subject: math
add.name: For every one, two
add.covers: For every 1 cup of rice, 2 cups of water: keeping a recipe or a bead pattern the same while making more of it; doubling and halving both parts; tables of matching amounts. The child can keep a 'for every' rule going and spot when a mixture has gone wrong.

add.subject: math
add.name: Fractions are numbers on the line
add.covers: Fractions placed on the number line between 0 and 1 and beyond: 5/4 is past 1; counting in halves, quarters and thirds; mixed numbers and improper fractions as two names for one point; which whole number a fraction is nearest. The child can place any simple fraction on a line and name a point on it.

add.subject: math
add.name: Calculating with fractions
add.covers: Adding and subtracting fractions with different denominators by finding a common one; a fraction times a whole number; a fraction of a fraction (half of a third) with paper folding and the area picture; dividing by a unit fraction as 'how many quarters fit in 3?'. The child can do all four and explain, with a picture, why multiplying by a fraction below 1 makes a number smaller.

add.subject: math
add.name: Calculating with decimals
add.covers: Adding and subtracting decimals to three places; multiplying and dividing by 10, 100 and 1000 as digits shifting place; a decimal times a whole number and a decimal times a decimal (0.3 × 0.2 with a hundred square); estimating to place the decimal point. The child can calculate bills and measurements with decimals and judge whether the answer is the right size.

add.subject: math
add.name: Percentages
add.covers: Percent as 'out of 100'; 50%, 25%, 10% and 1% of an amount, and any percentage built from these; discounts and marks out of a total; changing between fractions, decimals and percentages; a rise of 10% followed by a fall of 10% does not return to the start. The child can find a percentage of an amount, write one number as a percentage of another, and explain the rise-and-fall surprise.

add.subject: math
add.name: Best buy: the price for one
add.covers: Which pack is cheaper? Finding the price for one item, one kilogram or 100 grams and comparing; offers such as 'buy 2 get 1 free' worked out honestly; when the bigger pack is not the better buy. The child can compare two prices fairly and explain the choice.

add.subject: math
add.name: Money that grows: interest
add.covers: Saving and borrowing: simple interest as a percentage of the amount each year; a table of savings year by year; interest added on interest (compound) and how it slowly pulls ahead; what a loan really costs. The child can work out simple interest, build a year-by-year table, and compare two savings plans.

add.subject: math
add.name: Rectangle numbers
add.covers: Which numbers of tiles can be laid as a rectangle, and in how many ways? 12 makes 1 × 12, 2 × 6 and 3 × 4; 7 makes only a single line. Multiples as the numbers in a times table. The child can find all the rectangles for numbers to 30 and sort numbers by how many rectangles they make.

add.subject: math
add.name: Prime numbers and the sieve
add.covers: Numbers with exactly two factors; why 1 is not counted as prime (an agreement that keeps other rules tidy); the sieve of Eratosthenes on a hundred square, crossing out multiples to leave the 25 primes below 100; patterns and gaps among them. The child can test a number below 100 for being prime and run the sieve.

add.subject: math
add.name: Primes never end
add.covers: Every whole number above 1 breaks into primes in exactly one way (factor trees that always end with the same primes). Euclid's proof, in plain steps, that the primes never run out: multiply all the primes you have, add 1, and the new number needs a prime you did not have. Questions nobody has settled yet: twin primes and Goldbach's guess. The child can write a number as a product of primes and retell Euclid's argument.

add.subject: math
add.name: Divisibility tests
add.covers: Quick tests for 2, 5 and 10 (the last digit), 4 (the last two digits), and 3 and 9 (the sum of the digits), found by sorting numbers and looking for what they share. The child can tell without dividing whether a number up to 9999 divides by these.

add.subject: math
add.name: Why the divisibility tests work
add.covers: Tests for 6, 8, 11 and 12 added to the earlier ones, and the reasons behind them all: 10, 100 and 1000 each leave remainder 1 on dividing by 9, so a number and its digit sum leave the same remainder; casting out nines to check a sum. The child can explain the test for 9 with place value and build a test for 6 from the tests for 2 and 3.

add.subject: math
add.name: Highest common factor, lowest common multiple
add.covers: The largest square tile that exactly covers a 12 by 18 floor (HCF) and the first time two bells ring together (LCM); finding both from lists and from prime factors; Euclid's method of cutting the biggest square off a rectangle again and again; the product of two numbers equals HCF × LCM. The child can find the HCF and LCM of two numbers and choose which one a problem needs.

add.subject: math
add.name: What comes next? Number patterns
add.covers: Patterns in counting with objects and on a number track: one more each time, two more each time, one fewer; staircases of blocks; saying what comes next and what is missing. The child can continue a simple growing or shrinking pattern and say what changes each time.

add.subject: math
add.name: Growing shape patterns
add.covers: Patterns that grow instead of repeat: staircases, growing squares and triangles of counters, L-shapes; counting how many are added each time; building the next two shapes. The child can tell a repeating pattern from a growing one and build the next step.

add.subject: math
add.name: Predicting far along a pattern
add.covers: In a red, blue, green bead pattern, what colour is the 20th bead? The 100th? Using the length of the repeating unit and counting in multiples; patterns with two things changing at once (colour every 2, shape every 3). The child can predict any position in a repeating pattern without drawing it all.

add.subject: math
add.name: Fibonacci numbers and spirals
add.covers: The sequence where each number is the sum of the two before it (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 ...). It appears in Indian writing on poetic rhythm (the ways to fill a line with short and long beats), set out by Virahanka and later Hemachandra, before Fibonacci's rabbit puzzle of 1202. Counting the spirals on a pine cone, a pineapple and a sunflower head. The child can build the sequence, count the long-and-short rhythms for lines up to 6 beats, and count spirals on a real plant.

add.subject: math
add.name: The triangle of numbers (Meru Prastara)
add.covers: The triangle where each number is the sum of the two above it, described in India as Meru Prastara (Halayudha, 10th century, explaining Pingala) and known in Europe as Pascal's triangle. Patterns inside it: the counting numbers, the triangle numbers, rows that add up to powers of 2, Fibonacci numbers along slanted lines, and the triangle-within-triangle picture made by colouring the odd numbers. Each number counts the routes to that spot. The child can build ten rows, find five patterns, and explain why the rows double.

add.subject: math
add.name: The same on both sides
add.covers: The equals sign means 'is the same as', not 'the answer comes next': a pan balance with blocks; 3 + 2 balances 4 + 1; making a balance level by adding or taking away. The child can say whether two sides are equal and fix them if they are not.

add.subject: math
add.name: Solving balance puzzles
add.covers: One-step equations with a shape or a letter for the unknown, with all four operations (n + 27 = 63, 6 × n = 54, n ÷ 4 = 9); solving by doing the same to both sides of a balance and by using the inverse operation; writing an equation for a short story. The child can solve one-step equations and check each answer by putting it back.

add.subject: math
add.name: Number machines
add.covers: A machine that does one thing to every number that goes in (add 3, take away 2, double): feeding numbers through, filling a table of ins and outs, and being the machine for a partner. The child can run a one-step machine forwards and fill its table.

add.subject: math
add.name: Two-step machines, forwards and backwards
add.covers: Machines with two steps (multiply by 3, then add 2); finding the rule from a table; running a machine backwards by undoing the steps in reverse order; why 'add 2 then multiply by 3' is a different machine. The child can find a two-step rule and work back from an output to its input.

add.subject: math
add.name: Letters for numbers
add.covers: A letter standing for any number, not one hidden number: the perimeter of a square is 4 × s whatever s is; writing a pattern rule with a letter; putting numbers in place of the letter; 'n + 3' as an answer in its own right. The child can write a rule in words and with a letter, and work out its value for a given number.

add.subject: math
add.name: Expressions: collecting and expanding
add.covers: Writing without the times sign (3a, ab); collecting like terms (3a + 2a = 5a, but 3a + 2b stays as it is); brackets opened with the area picture (2 × (a + 3) = 2a + 6); putting in values using the order of operations; two expressions that look different and are always equal. The child can simplify, expand a single bracket, and test whether two expressions are the same.

add.subject: math
add.name: Formulas
add.covers: A formula as a rule written once for every case: area = l × b, perimeter = 2 × (l + b), distance = speed × time, cost = price × number + delivery; putting values in; finding the missing quantity when the answer is known; making a formula for a real job at home. The child can use a formula, turn a simple one round to find another quantity, and write one of her own.

add.subject: math
add.name: Graphs of rules
add.covers: From rule to table to points on a coordinate grid: rules like y = 2x + 1 make a straight line; what the multiplier does (steepness) and what the added number does (where the line starts); reading answers off the graph; where two lines cross and what that means; a rule like y = x × x makes a curve. The child can draw the graph of a simple rule and tell the rule from a straight-line graph.

add.subject: math
add.name: More than, less than, with letters
add.covers: Statements with many answers: n + 3 > 10; showing all the answers on a number line; 'at least', 'at most', 'between'; solving simple inequalities by the balance idea; real limits (a lift that carries at most 400 kg). The child can write an inequality for a situation, solve it, and show the answers on a line.

add.subject: math
add.name: Two unknowns at once
add.covers: Puzzles with two hidden numbers and two clues: hens and goats with 10 heads and 28 legs; two numbers with a given sum and difference. Solved three ways: an orderly table of tries, a picture (give every animal two legs first), and two balance equations where one is taken from the other. The child can solve a two-clue puzzle and explain why one clue alone is not enough.

add.subject: math
add.name: Shapes made from shapes
add.covers: Putting shapes together and cutting them apart: two triangles make a square, a rectangle or a bigger triangle; pictures from tangram-like pieces; folding and cutting a square into halves and quarters in different ways. The child can make a named shape from smaller ones and find shapes hidden inside a bigger one.

add.subject: math
add.name: Circles and the compass
add.covers: What makes a circle: every point the same distance from the centre; drawing circles with string and with a compass; centre, radius and diameter, and diameter = 2 × radius; flower and kolam designs from overlapping circles. The child can draw a circle of a given radius and explain why a wheel is round.

add.subject: math
add.name: Pi: around and across
add.covers: Measuring round and across lids, plates and wheels with string: the distance round is always a little more than 3 times the distance across. That number is pi; circumference = pi × diameter. Aryabhata gave 3.1416, and Madhava of Kerala found a way to get as close as you like with an endless sum. Pi cannot be written exactly as a fraction or a finished decimal. The child can find pi by measuring, use it to find a circumference, and say why her measured value is only close.

add.subject: math
add.name: Same shape and same size
add.covers: Two shapes are congruent if one fits exactly on the other after sliding, turning or flipping; testing by tracing; shapes that look alike but fail the test; how many different triangles can be made on a 3 by 3 pin-board, once flips and turns count as the same. The child can test for congruence and say which moves she used.

add.subject: math
add.name: Similar shapes and scale factor
add.covers: Shapes with the same shape but a different size: every length multiplied by the same number (the scale factor) and every angle unchanged; enlarging a drawing on a grid; finding a missing side; when lengths double, area becomes 4 times as big, seen by counting squares. The child can enlarge a shape by a scale factor, test two shapes for similarity, and predict the new area.

add.subject: math
add.name: Drawing exactly: ruler and compass
add.covers: Constructions with only a straight edge and a compass: an equilateral triangle, a regular hexagon inside a circle, a line cut exactly in half at right angles, an angle cut in half, a triangle from three given sides; why three lengths do not always make a triangle (the two short sides must together be longer than the third). The child can carry out each construction and explain why the compass guarantees equal lengths.

add.subject: math
add.name: The right-angle rule
add.covers: In a right-angled triangle, the squares drawn on the two short sides together have the same area as the square on the long side: found by drawing on squared paper, shown by a cut-and-rearrange proof. The rule is stated in the Baudhayana Sulba Sutra of ancient India (as the rule for the diagonal of a rectangle), was used in Babylon, and is named after Pythagoras in Europe. The 3-4-5 rope for making a true corner. The child can test whether a triangle is right-angled, find the long side for simple whole-number cases, and retell the rearrangement proof.

add.subject: math
add.name: Prisms and pyramids
add.covers: Sorting solids into families: prisms (the same shape all the way through) and pyramids (sides meeting at a point), named by their base; cylinders and cones as their round cousins; building them from straws and clay. The child can name a prism or pyramid from its base and describe a solid well enough for someone else to build it.

add.subject: math
add.name: Euler's rule for solids
add.covers: A table of faces, corners and edges for many solids shows one rule: faces + corners − edges = 2 (found by Euler). Testing it on prisms, pyramids and a cut-off cube; solids with a hole, where it fails; the only five solids whose faces are all the same regular shape (the Platonic solids), made from nets. The child can check Euler's rule on any solid without holes and use it to find a missing count.

add.subject: math
add.name: Slicing solids
add.covers: What shape appears when a solid is cut? Slicing clay or vegetables: a cylinder gives circles, rectangles and ovals; a cube can give a triangle, a square, a rectangle and even a hexagon; a cone gives a circle or an oval. Predict first, then cut. The child can predict and draw the slice a given cut will make.

add.subject: math
add.name: Building from views
add.covers: Front, side and top views of a cube building; building a model that matches three given views, and finding that more than one building can match; drawing solids on dotted (isometric) paper; the most and the fewest cubes a set of views allows. The child can draw the three views of a model and build a model from its views.

add.subject: math
add.name: Turning
add.covers: Whole turns and half turns made with the body, a door and a clock hand; turning to the left and to the right, clockwise and anticlockwise; where you face after a turn. The child can make and describe whole and half turns.

add.subject: math
add.name: Points, lines and crossings
add.covers: A point, a line and a line segment; measuring and drawing segments with a ruler; lines that cross and lines that never meet, found in letters, railway tracks and woven mats; counting the crossing points made by 2, 3 and 4 lines. The child can draw and measure segments and describe how two lines lie.

add.subject: math
add.name: Angles where lines cross
add.covers: Angles on a straight line add up to 180 degrees and angles round a point to 360; when two lines cross, the opposite angles are equal, and why; a line crossing two parallel lines makes matching equal angles (found by tracing and sliding). The child can find missing angles at a crossing and with parallel lines, giving a reason for each step.

add.subject: math
add.name: Measuring angles in degrees
add.covers: Using a protractor to measure and draw angles to the nearest degree; angles bigger than a straight line (reflex); estimating an angle before measuring; why a full turn is 360 (a choice that goes back to Babylon's counting in sixties); angles of clock hands and of a ramp. The child can measure, draw and estimate angles of any size.

add.subject: math
add.name: Angle sums in triangles and polygons
add.covers: Tearing off the three corners of any paper triangle and fitting them on a straight line: 180 degrees every time, and a proof using a line parallel to one side; four-sided shapes give 360; any polygon splits into triangles, so the sum is (sides − 2) × 180; walking round a shape, the turns add up to one full turn. The child can find a missing angle in a triangle or polygon and explain the triangle proof.

add.subject: math
add.name: Shadows and heights
add.covers: At the same moment, a stick twice as tall throws a shadow twice as long: measuring sticks and their shadows through a morning and recording them in a table; using the pattern to find the height of a pole or a tree. The child can find a height from two shadows and one known stick.

add.subject: math
add.name: Mirror lines
add.covers: Finding the mirror line with a small mirror and by folding; finishing the missing half of a picture on squared and dotted paper; shapes with no mirror line, one, or more; symmetric kolam on a dot grid. The child can complete a symmetric figure and test a shape for mirror lines.

add.subject: math
add.name: Slide, flip and turn with cut-outs
add.covers: Moving a cut-out shape three ways: sliding it, flipping it over and turning it; saying which move was made; a border pattern made by repeating one move; a letter F shows the difference between a flip and a turn. The child can make each move and tell which one took a shape to its new place.

add.subject: math
add.name: Moving shapes with coordinates
add.covers: Describing moves with numbers: a slide as 'so many right, so many up' added to every corner's coordinates; a flip in an axis changes one sign; a quarter turn about the origin; two moves in a row and whether the order matters; all three keep size and shape. The child can carry out and describe a move on a coordinate grid and predict the new coordinates.

add.subject: math
add.name: Border patterns: only seven kinds
add.covers: Sari borders, temple carvings and kolam borders repeat along a strip. Sorting them by the moves that leave them unchanged (slide, flip across, flip along, half turn, slide-and-flip like footprints) gives exactly seven kinds and no more, a result mathematicians have proved. The child sorts real borders into the seven kinds and designs one of each from a single motif.

add.subject: math
add.name: Seen from above: plans and picture maps
add.covers: The view from above: drawing the plan of a table top, then of a room; picture maps of the way to a friend's house with landmarks in order; matching a plan to the real place. The child can draw a simple plan and follow someone else's.

add.subject: math
add.name: Points on a grid
add.covers: Naming a point by two numbers, across first and then up; points on the grid lines, not in the squares; plotting and reading points with whole numbers; a sea-battle game; joining points to make shapes. The child can plot and read coordinates and explain why the order of the two numbers matters.

add.subject: math
add.name: Compass directions and bearings
add.covers: Eight compass points; a direction given as an angle turned clockwise from north (a bearing); giving a route as distances and bearings and drawing it to scale; instructions for a walking 'robot' that draws squares, triangles and stars. The child can measure and follow a bearing and write turn-and-step instructions for a shape.

add.subject: math
add.name: Finding any place on Earth
add.covers: Coordinates on a ball: latitude as the angle north or south of the equator and longitude as the angle east or west of the Greenwich line; finding cities on a globe; why the longitude lines meet at the poles while latitude circles get smaller; longitude and the time of day. The child can find a place from its latitude and longitude and give the rough position of her own town.

add.subject: math
add.name: Benchmarks and nearest marks
add.covers: Personal benchmarks (my hand span is about 15 cm, a full water bottle is about 1 kg) used to estimate; measuring to the nearest unit and half unit; why two careful people can get slightly different results. The child can estimate with a benchmark and say how close her measurement is.

add.subject: math
add.name: The metric system and other systems
add.covers: One pattern for all metric units: kilo means 1000, centi a hundredth, milli a thousandth; converting with decimals by shifting digits; units people still use beside it (inches and feet, a tola of gold, an acre) and rough conversions; why the world agreed on shared units. The child can convert between metric units with decimals and explain what the prefixes mean.

add.subject: math
add.name: Weighing with a balance
add.covers: Comparing and ordering three or more things by weight on a pan balance; weighing with marbles or coins as units; big things can be light and small things heavy; meeting the kilogram as the weight of a litre bottle of water. The child can order objects by weight and say how many units each weighs.

add.subject: math
add.name: How many cups fill it?
add.covers: Measuring how much a vessel holds by counting cupfuls; tall and thin against short and wide: the same water looks different in different vessels; ordering vessels by how much they hold; meeting the litre. The child can measure capacity in cupfuls and explain why the height of the water alone can mislead.

add.subject: math
add.name: Heavy for its size
add.covers: Why a small stone outweighs a big sponge: weight for each cubic centimetre (density) found by weighing and measuring volume; water as the benchmark, 1 gram for each cubic centimetre; things denser than water sink and less dense things float. The child can work out a density from weight and volume and predict floating or sinking.

add.subject: math
add.name: Who is faster?
add.covers: Comparing speeds fairly: the same distance in less time, or more distance in the same time; what 'kilometres in an hour' means; walking, cycling and bus speeds measured or looked up; a table of distance against time for a steady walker. The child can decide who is faster from distances and times and say what a speed of 40 km in an hour tells us.

add.subject: math
add.name: Speed, distance and time
add.covers: Speed = distance ÷ time, and the same fact turned round to find distance or time; kilometres per hour and metres per second; average speed for a journey with stops (not the average of the speeds); reading a journey from a distance-time graph, where steeper means faster and flat means stopped. The child can find any one of speed, distance and time from the other two and tell the story of a distance-time graph.

add.subject: math
add.name: Time around the world
add.covers: Why it is morning in Chennai while it is still night in London: the Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours, 15 degrees each hour; time zones and Indian Standard Time, 5 and a half hours ahead of Greenwich; working out the time in another city; the date line. The child can find the time in another zone and explain why time zones are an agreement laid over the Earth's turning.

add.subject: math
add.name: Recording temperature
add.covers: Reading a thermometer to the nearest degree; benchmark temperatures (ice 0, the body about 37, boiling water 100 degrees Celsius); recording morning and afternoon temperatures for a week and finding the differences; first look below zero in cold places. The child can read and record temperatures and work out a rise or fall.

add.subject: math
add.name: Walking the edge
add.covers: The distance all the way round: walking the edge of a mat, laying string round a leaf and measuring it, counting unit edges round shapes on squared paper; shapes made of the same 6 squares can have different edges. The child can find the distance round a shape by measuring or counting.

add.subject: math
add.name: Filling boxes with cubes
add.covers: How many cubes fill a box? Building cuboids from unit cubes; counting one layer and then the number of layers; different boxes that hold the same number of cubes; space filled (volume) told apart from surface covered (area). The child can find the volume of a cuboid by counting layers of cubes.

add.subject: math
add.name: Area of triangles and parallelograms
add.covers: Cutting and rearranging to find a formula: a parallelogram becomes a rectangle with the same base and height; any triangle is half of a parallelogram, so its area is half of base × height; triangles with the same base and height have the same area even when they look different; finding areas on a grid and from measurements. The child can find these areas and explain each formula by cutting paper.

add.subject: math
add.name: Area of a circle
add.covers: Counting squares inside circles of different radius shows the area is a little more than 3 times radius × radius; cutting a circle into thin slices and laying them head to tail makes nearly a rectangle, half the circumference long and one radius high, which gives area = pi × radius × radius; thinner slices make it closer. The child can estimate and calculate the area of a circle and explain the slice argument.

add.subject: math
add.name: The middle and the most
add.covers: One number to stand for a whole set: the mode (the value that comes up most) and the median (the middle one when all are lined up in order); the range from smallest to largest; heights, shoe sizes and scores at home. The child can find the mode, median and range of a small set and say what each tells us.

add.subject: math
add.name: The mean, and which average to trust
add.covers: The mean as levelling out: sharing towers of cubes until all are equal, then total ÷ number; how one extreme value drags the mean but hardly moves the median; choosing the mean, median or mode for a purpose (shoe sizes to stock, typical pay, a batting average); two sets with the same mean and very different spread. The child can calculate a mean, choose a suitable average, and use the range to compare how spread out two sets are.

add.subject: math
add.name: Pie charts
add.covers: A whole circle shared out: reading pie charts in halves, quarters, tenths and percentages; drawing one with a protractor (each share as a part of 360 degrees); a pie chart shows shares, not amounts, so two pies of different totals cannot be compared slice for slice. The child can read and draw a pie chart and say when a bar chart would be better.

add.subject: math
add.name: Dot plots and grouped data
add.covers: When there are too many different values for one bar each: dot plots on a number line; grouping measurements into equal class intervals (heights 120 to 129 cm, 130 to 139 cm); how the choice of groups changes the picture; the shape of the data: where most values sit and where the stragglers are. The child can group measured data, draw the chart, and describe its shape.

add.subject: math
add.name: Do two things go together? Scatter graphs
add.covers: One dot for each person or thing, placed by two measurements (height and arm span, hours of sun and plant growth); dots rising together, falling, or showing no link; drawing a line through the middle of the cloud and using it to predict; two things going together does not show that one causes the other. The child can draw and read a scatter graph and give an example where a link is not a cause.

add.subject: math
add.name: Asking a few to learn about many
add.covers: We cannot ask everyone, so we ask a sample: tasting one spoonful of well-stirred sambar; estimating the colours in a big bag of beads from a handful, then from a larger handful; how a sample goes wrong (asking only friends, a leading question, too few); how surveys and counts of wild animals use sampling. The child can plan a fair sample, estimate from it, and name what could bias it.

add.subject: math
add.name: Which comes up most?
add.covers: First chance experiments: tossing a coin 20 times, pulling beads from a bag with more red than blue, a spinner with unequal parts; predicting first, tallying, and comparing with the prediction; the result is not the same each time the experiment is repeated. The child can run a simple chance experiment, record it, and link 'more of them' with 'comes up more often'.

add.subject: math
add.name: Listing everything that can happen
add.covers: Finding all the outcomes without missing or repeating any: two coins (four outcomes, not three), a coin and a dice, two spinners; orderly lists and two-way tables; counting how many of the outcomes give what we want. The child can list all outcomes of two simple events and explain why 'one head and one tail' is twice as likely as 'two heads'.

add.subject: math
add.name: Chance as a number
add.covers: When all outcomes are equally likely, the chance of an event is the number of ways it can happen out of the number of outcomes: a fraction from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain); written also as a decimal and a percentage; the chance of it not happening is 1 minus the chance that it does; cards, dice, and names drawn from a bowl. The child can work out a probability, place it on the 0 to 1 line, and find the chance of the opposite event.

add.subject: math
add.name: Two events: tables and tree diagrams
add.covers: The 36 outcomes of two dice in a grid, and why a total of 7 is the most likely; tree diagrams for two and three coin tosses; chances found by counting branches, and for simple cases by multiplying along a branch (1/2 × 1/2); a tree where the branches are not equal (a bag with 3 red and 1 blue). The child can draw a table or tree for two events and find the chance of a combined result.

add.subject: math
add.name: The long run
add.covers: Ten tosses can give 7 heads; a thousand tosses come very close to half. Collecting results from many throws and plotting the fraction of heads as the count grows; chance says little about the next toss and a great deal about the long run (the law of large numbers); the coin has no memory, so a run of tails does not make heads 'due'. The child can show the fraction settling with her own data and explain the gambler's mistake.

add.subject: math
add.name: Is the game worth playing?
add.covers: A stall game: pay 10 rupees, roll a dice, win 30 rupees on a six. Working out the average result for each turn over many turns (expected value) from the chances and the prizes; changing the prize to make the game fair; why lotteries and fairground games are built so the organiser gains over the long run; insurance as the same sum seen from the other side. The child can work out the expected value of a simple game and design a fair one.

add.subject: math
add.name: Puzzles with clues
add.covers: Who lives where? Puzzles solved from two or three clues; simple number riddles (I am between 10 and 20 and you say me when counting in fives); matchstick and shape-count puzzles. The child can use each clue in turn and explain how she knows.

add.subject: math
add.name: River crossings and weighing puzzles
add.covers: Classic puzzles that need a plan: the farmer, goat, tiger and grass crossing a river; finding the one heavier coin among nine in two weighings on a balance; pouring exactly 4 litres with a 3-litre and a 5-litre pot. Recording the moves and looking for the shortest way. The child can solve such a puzzle, record the solution, and argue that no shorter one exists for a small case.

add.subject: math
add.name: Work in order: lists and tables
add.covers: Being systematic: finding all the ways to make 20 rupees from 5 and 10 rupee coins, all the 3-digit numbers from three digit cards, all the ways to split 10 into three parts; an orderly list shows when every answer has been found. The child can list all the possibilities in order and say why none is missing.

add.subject: math
add.name: Counting without missing any
add.covers: Tree diagrams and the multiplication rule: 3 snacks and 4 drinks give 3 × 4 choices; adding a third choice multiplies again; handshakes among 5 people counted in an orderly way (4 + 3 + 2 + 1) and why each handshake must be counted once. The child can count choices by multiplying and count pairs without double counting.

add.subject: math
add.name: Sets: and, or, not
add.covers: A set as a clearly described collection; the overlap (in both), the union (in at least one) and the outside (in neither); survey puzzles with two circles (18 like cricket, 12 like football, 5 like both, 3 like neither: how many children?) and why adding the two groups counts some twice; sets of numbers inside sets (squares inside whole numbers). The child can solve a two-circle counting problem and describe a region with and, or, not.

add.subject: math
add.name: And, or, not: the logic inside computers
add.covers: Statements joined by and, or, not, and when the joined statement is true (truth tables with 1 and 0); the same tables built with switches in a torch circuit, in a row for 'and' and side by side for 'or'; how such simple gates, in huge numbers, let a computer add in binary. The child can fill a truth table for a simple combined statement and build an 'and' and an 'or' with switches.

add.subject: math
add.name: One-line drawings
add.covers: Can you draw it without lifting the pencil or going over a line twice? Trying houses, stars and envelopes; kolam drawn as one unbroken loop; sorting figures into possible and impossible. The child can test a figure by trying and sort a set of figures.

add.subject: math
add.name: The bridges of Königsberg
add.covers: The seven bridges puzzle that Leonhard Euler settled in 1736: turning a map into dots and lines; counting the lines at each dot; a walk using every line once is possible only when no dot, or exactly two dots, have an odd number of lines. Checking the rule on the one-line drawings from before. The child can turn a map into a network and decide, without trying every route, whether such a walk exists.

add.subject: math
add.name: Maps, colours and shortest routes
add.covers: Networks at work: the shortest route between two towns on a map with distances; the cheapest way to join all the villages with a pipe; colouring a map so that no neighbours match, and the four-colour theorem: four colours are always enough, proved in 1976 with the help of a computer, which started an argument about what counts as a proof. The child can find a shortest route on a small network, colour a map with as few colours as possible, and say what the four-colour theorem claims.

add.subject: math
add.name: Convince me: what a proof is
add.covers: The difference between 'it worked every time I tried' and 'it must always work': odd + odd is always even, shown with pairs of dots and one left over; the sum of three numbers in a row is always 3 times the middle one; a pattern that looks true and then breaks (the regions made by joining points on a circle: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, then 31). The child can give a picture proof of a simple number fact and explain why examples alone are not a proof.

add.subject: math
add.name: Proof, starting rules, and what cannot be proved
add.covers: Three kinds of proof met in this level's units: by picture, by a chain of reasons, and by showing that the opposite leads to nonsense (Euclid on primes). Every proof stands on starting rules (axioms) that are accepted, not proved; change a starting rule and a different, equally sound mathematics follows. 'This sentence is false' and why it traps us. Then Kurt Gödel's finding of 1931, in plain and honest words: in any consistent set of rules strong enough for arithmetic, there are true statements the rules cannot prove. This shows a limit of rule systems; it does not by itself show that maths is only opinion. The child can tell a proof from evidence, name an axiom, and say in her own words what Gödel found and what it does not say.

add.subject: math
add.name: Step-by-step recipes: algorithms
add.covers: An algorithm is a list of exact steps that anyone can follow without thinking: instructions for a 'robot' parent to draw a shape; the steps for column addition seen as an algorithm; sorting number cards by swapping neighbours; finding and fixing a wrong step. The child can write clear steps for a simple task, follow someone else's exactly, and find the mistake in a broken set.

add.subject: math
add.name: Fast and slow algorithms
add.covers: Two ways to do the same job can differ enormously in work: guessing a number from 1 to 100 one by one, or by halving (never more than 7 guesses), and how doubling the range adds only one guess; sorting cards two ways and counting the comparisons; Euclid's way to find a highest common factor as a very old, fast algorithm. The child can use the halving search, count the steps of an algorithm, and compare two methods by their step counts.

add.subject: math
add.name: Games with a winning plan
add.covers: Games with no luck in them: noughts and crosses (two careful players always draw), the race to 21 (add 1, 2 or 3 each turn), and a small game of Nim with heaps of stones; finding the winning plan by starting from the end and working backwards. The child can play these games with a plan and explain why the plan cannot lose.

add.subject: math
add.name: Patterns on living things
add.covers: Looking closely and counting: petals on flowers, legs on insects and spiders, stripes and spots, the two matching halves of a butterfly or a leaf, the spiral of a snail shell. The child can find, count and draw a pattern on a real plant or animal.

add.subject: math
add.name: Animal builders
add.covers: Shapes that animals build: the six-sided cells of a honeycomb, the spokes and spiral of an orb spider's web, the woven nest of a baya weaver bird. Looking at pictures or the real thing, counting sides and spokes, and copying the shapes with sticks and thread. The child can name the shapes in an animal's building and make a model of one.
verify: Check each animal example against a real source when the unit is written (web structure, weaver nest).

add.subject: math
add.name: Do animals count?
add.covers: What careful experiments have found: Saharan desert ants judge the distance home by their steps (ants given longer legs walked too far, ants with shortened legs stopped short; Wittlinger, Wehner and Wolf, 2006); honeybees and some birds can tell small numbers apart. What 'counting' means, and whether this is counting as we do it or something else. The child can retell one experiment, say what it showed, and say what it did not show.
verify: The honeybee and bird number-sense claims need a named study each before they are printed.

add.subject: math
add.name: Why hexagons?
add.covers: Which shapes cover a flat surface with no gaps (triangles, squares, hexagons) and which of them needs the least wall for the same room inside: the child measures the edges of each for equal areas and finds the hexagon wins. Mathematicians guessed for about two thousand years that nothing beats the hexagon grid; Thomas Hales proved it in 1999. Honeycomb, soap bubbles pressed together and drying mud show the same shape. The child can compare shapes by edge length for the same area and explain why a honeycomb saves wax.

add.subject: math
add.name: Size, shape and growth in living things
add.covers: Why an ant can carry many times its weight and an elephant needs thick legs: when a shape is made twice as long, its surface becomes 4 times and its volume and weight 8 times as big (noticed by Galileo), tested with cubes and clay. How seeds pack a sunflower head: each new seed turns by the same angle, about 137.5 degrees, and the Fibonacci spirals appear. A shell that keeps its shape as it grows. The child can work out how area and volume change with size and explain one way that sets limits on living bodies.

add.subject: math
add.name: Beats and steps
add.covers: Counting in music and dance: clapping cycles of 3 beats and of 4 beats; strong and weak beats; steps that repeat on each side; the lines and circles dancers form. The child can keep a beat cycle going, say which beat she is on, and make up a short step pattern that repeats.

add.subject: math
add.name: Tala: the maths of rhythm
add.covers: Rhythm cycles of Indian music: Adi tala with 8 beats grouped 4 + 2 + 2, Rupaka, and cycles of 5 and 7; clapping two different cycles together and finding when they next start together (the lowest common multiple); filling a cycle with long (2-beat) and short (1-beat) sounds and counting the ways, which gives the Fibonacci numbers. The child can clap a tala with its grouping, predict when two cycles meet, and count the rhythms for a short cycle.
verify: Check the beat groupings and names of the talas with a music source when the unit is written.

add.subject: math
add.name: Why notes sound good together
add.covers: Stretching a string or rubber band over a box: half the length sounds the same note an octave higher (2 to 1); two-thirds of the length gives the note called Pa in Indian music, a fifth above (3 to 2); simple ratios sound restful together and complicated ones clash. Different cultures divide the octave differently, so a scale is a choice built on a fact about ratios. The child can find the octave and the fifth on a string by measuring and explain a musical interval as a ratio.

add.subject: math
add.name: Maths in stitching and weaving
add.covers: Over one, under one: weaving paper strips and reading the pattern; running stitch and cross stitch counted on squared cloth or paper; a border that repeats; what happens when the count goes wrong by one. The child can follow and make a counted pattern in weaving or stitching.

add.subject: math
add.name: Keeping score
add.covers: The numbers inside games: 6 balls to an over in cricket, points and bonus points in kabaddi, turns and chases in kho-kho; keeping a tally score sheet for a real game; working out totals, leads and how many are needed to win. The child can keep the score of a game and answer questions from the score sheet.

add.subject: math
add.name: The numbers behind sport
add.covers: What sports numbers mean and hide: a batting average, a strike rate (runs for every 100 balls) and a run rate; the required rate in a chase; speed from a race time; the angle of a shot or a pass; whether a 'best player' depends on which number you choose. The child can calculate these rates and averages from a real scorecard and argue which number is fairest for a question.

add.subject: math
add.name: Puzzle makers and number lovers
add.covers: Bhaskara II, who wrote his sums as riddles about bees, pearls and peacocks in the Lilavati (about 1150); the story told of the schoolboy Gauss adding 1 to 100 by pairing (a story, not a certain fact, but the method is real); Shakuntala Devi, who calculated in her head on stage. Trying one puzzle and one method from each. The child can retell one story and use the pairing trick to add 1 to 20.
verify: Check the Lilavati date and the Shakuntala Devi details when the unit is written; keep the Gauss story marked as a story.

add.subject: math
add.name: From Aryabhata to Ramanujan
add.covers: A line of Indian mathematics with what each person found: Aryabhata (born 476), who gave pi as 3.1416 and said the Earth turns; Brahmagupta (628), who wrote rules for zero and negative numbers; Bhaskara II and the Lilavati; Madhava of Sangamagrama in Kerala (about 1340 to 1425), credited by his followers with endless sums for pi, about 250 years before the same sums were found in Europe; Ramanujan (1887 to 1920), who filled notebooks with results from a small town in Tamil Nadu, and the number 1729. What is well recorded, what rests on later writers, and how ideas travelled both ways. The child can match each person to a finding, try one piece of each (a few terms of Madhava's sum, the two ways to write 1729 as two cubes), and say what we do not know.
verify: Give the Aryabhatiya's date (usually 499 CE) only after checking it; Madhava's sums are known through later Kerala writers, so say 'credited with'.

add.subject: math
add.name: Who decided? Maths has agreements
add.covers: Some things in maths are agreements people made: the shapes of the digits, the signs + and =, counting in tens, the length of a metre. Other things are found and stay true whatever we agree: 2 and 3 make 5 in any language, with any signs. Writing a sum with invented signs; counting in another language at home. The child can sort simple examples into 'people agreed' and 'true anyway' and give a reason.

add.subject: math
add.name: What counts as the same?
add.covers: Maths begins with choices about what to treat as the same: 1/2 and 2/4 are the same number; a square turned on its corner is the same shape; on a clock 13 and 1 are the same hour; is a shape and its mirror image the same? Changing one rule of a known game or of arithmetic (work on a 12-hour clock) and following what happens. The child can name what is being ignored when two things are called equal and follow a changed rule to its results.

add.subject: math
add.name: Patterns inside patterns
add.covers: A fern leaf is made of small leaves shaped like the whole leaf; a cauliflower floret looks like a small cauliflower; a branch looks like a small tree. Looking with a magnifying glass, breaking off a piece and comparing it with the whole, and drawing a tree with one rule: every branch grows two smaller branches. The child can point to the small copy inside the whole and draw a branching tree by repeating one rule.

add.subject: math
add.name: Building fractals
add.covers: Making a fractal by repeating one step: the Sierpinski triangle (take out the middle triangle, again and again) and the Koch snowflake (put a bump on every side); counting the pieces at each stage (1, 3, 9, 27 ...) and the fraction of the area left (3/4, then 9/16); the same shape at every size. The child can draw three stages of a fractal and give the rule for the number of pieces.

add.subject: math
add.name: How long is a coastline?
add.covers: Each stage of the Koch snowflake has an edge 4/3 as long as the stage before, so the edge grows without limit while the area stays inside a circle you can draw round it. Measuring a wiggly coast on a map with a long step and then a short step: the shorter the ruler, the longer the coast, so 'the length' depends on how we choose to measure. Benoit Mandelbrot named such shapes fractals. Where nature is roughly fractal (coasts, rivers, lungs, lightning) and where the likeness ends. The child can calculate the Koch edge for several stages, measure a map coast two ways, and explain why the answers differ.
verify: Mandelbrot's coastline paper is usually dated 1967 and the word 'fractal' 1975; check before printing dates.

add.subject: math
add.name: Can we tell what will happen?
add.covers: Some things can be predicted long ahead (sunrise, the swing of a pendulum, the next full moon) and some cannot (where a falling leaf lands, how a dice falls), though all follow nature's rules. Timing a pendulum again and again against dropping a leaf again and again, and recording how alike the results are. The child can sort events into 'easy to predict' and 'hard to predict' and back the choice with her own measurements.

add.subject: math
add.name: Tiny change, big difference
add.covers: Starts that are almost the same and endings that are not: a marble let go from the top of an upturned bowl; a ball dropped through rows of pegs; a number game (double the number and, if it passes 1, drop the 1) played from 0.30 and from 0.31, where the two paths soon part. Next to it, a tame rule (add 2 each time) where a small difference stays small. The child can run both rules, chart them, and say what 'sensitive to the start' means.

add.subject: math
add.name: Chaos: exact rules, no long forecast
add.covers: Edward Lorenz, in 1961, typed .506 into his weather program in place of .506127 and before long the new forecast no longer matched the old one. Repeating the idea with a calculator: the rule 'new = 4 × old × (1 − old)' started at 0.300 and at 0.301. Each step is fixed exactly by the rule, with no luck in it, and yet tiny errors in the start grow until prediction fails: this is chaos, and it is why weather forecasts fade after some days while eclipses are known centuries ahead. The child can run the rule, graph the two runs, and explain how chaos differs from chance.

add.subject: math
add.name: The paper with one side
add.covers: A paper strip joined with a half twist (a Möbius strip): drawing a line down the middle comes back to the start having covered 'both' sides, so there is only one. Guessing and then cutting along the middle: one long band, not two. Cutting a plain loop for comparison. The child can make the strip, show it has one side and one edge, and predict then test a cut.

add.subject: math
add.name: Rubber-sheet geometry
add.covers: A geometry where stretching and bending are allowed but cutting and gluing are not: a clay ball can become a bowl but not a ring; counting holes (a vada and a cup with a handle each have one); inside and outside of a tangled closed loop; the Möbius strip again, cut one-third of the way from the edge; the strip was described by Möbius and by Listing in 1858. The child can sort objects by their number of holes and explain what this geometry ignores and what it keeps.

add.subject: math
add.name: Line, flat, solid: dimensions
add.covers: A line has length only; a flat shape has length and width; a solid has height as well. How many numbers fix a spot: one on a road, two on a floor, three in a room. An ant on a thread, an ant on a table, a fly in a room. The child can say how many dimensions an object or a movement has and why.

add.subject: math
add.name: Flatland and the fourth dimension
add.covers: How a flat creature would see a ball passing through its world: a dot, a growing circle, a shrinking circle, nothing. Building upward by a pattern: a point, a line (2 ends), a square (4 corners), a cube (8 corners), so a four-dimensional cube would have 16; drawing its shadow. Mathematicians can work in four or more dimensions by rule even though nobody can picture them. The child can continue the corner and edge patterns to four dimensions and explain a slice of a solid as what a flat creature would see.

add.subject: math
add.name: A flat page and a ball
add.covers: On a globe, the shortest way between two cities is found with a stretched string, and it is part of a great circle, not the straight line drawn on a flat map; why aeroplanes seem to fly curved routes; why every flat map of the Earth must stretch something (peeling an orange). The child can find the shortest route on a globe with string and explain why it looks curved on a map.

add.subject: math
add.name: Triangles on a ball
add.covers: On a ball, 'straight' lines are great circles. A triangle drawn on a globe from the north pole down to the equator, a quarter of the way round, and back has three right angles: 270 degrees, not 180. Two lines that start side by side at the equator meet at the pole, so there are no parallel lines. Euclid's rule about parallels is a starting rule that holds on a flat page; change it and another geometry follows, just as sound. Scientists use such geometries to describe the Earth's surface and space itself. The child can measure a triangle on a ball, compare it with one on paper, and explain that the 180-degree rule belongs to flat surfaces.

add.subject: math
add.name: Growing fast, growing slow
add.covers: Measuring something that changes every day (a bean shoot, a candle burning down, water dripping into a jar) and recording it in a table; how much it changed each day; steady change against change that speeds up or slows down. The child can find the change from one measurement to the next and say whether the change is steady.
